classification_signals: abstract: 'This paper examines CitySpinning, a public art project initiated by Prayas Abhinav... City Spinning is a series of interventions that incorporates unused and vacant spaces... The project re-interprets these spaces... making these spaces more configurable'
section: '6.2 CitySpinning' describes the framework and its aims.

section: '6.3 Ongoing Spins' describes specific, ongoing projects/interventions (Common Food, Know Me Know My News, Look At The Stars, The Muddy-hands Survey) rather than presenting completed empirical results.

conclusion: 'Creating engaging situations which are simple, fun and socially productive for them and at the same time get them involved in a mesh of wide-ranging concerns is a worthwhile pursuit.' This reflects a proposal for action rather than a report of findings.

findings.antecedent: CitySpinning interventions (based on free software and creative commons principles)
findings.quote: The project re-interprets these spaces with references borrowed from the free software movement and the creative commons movement, making these spaces more configurable

findings.antecedent: use of multiple sensors and collective ability to control sensory ambiance of space
findings.quote: The use of multiple sensors and the ability of the collective to control the sensory ambiance of space can help in creating more engaging experiences for individuals.

findings.antecedent: ongoing conversation between users of cities and planners/builders/architects
findings.source: Section 2. Indian Cities in Boomtime, p. 6
findings.quote: If there is an ongoing conversation between the users of cities (that is the citizens) and the planners, builders and architects, such expensive glitches might be avoided.

findings.consequent: everyday interaction and information flows (public life of cities)
findings.quote: Public space forms a vital conduit in this exchange process, providing platforms for everyday interaction and information flows – the basis and content for the public life of cities.”

findings.consequent: controls on free speech, political action, sanitized environment
findings.quote: These privately owned shared spaces have been able to exert controls which public spaces had great difficulty in exerting. Controls on free speech, political action... filter our undesirable and unwanted elements and create a “sanitized” environment.

findings.consequent: rethinking submission of urban space to commodity spectacle and surveillance, forging new ways of engaging with others in public
findings.quote: Scott McQuire suggests that Lozano-henner’s work involves strangers to suspend habits and try to figure out the interface and interplay of the project through experimentation. He uses this work as an example to describe the ways in which social inter-mingling and interaction is beginning to happen again in public spaces in the “media-city” and predicts that such projects “could become important tools for rethinking the submission of urban space to commodity spectacle and surveillance, and for forging new ways of engaging with others in public.”

findings.consequent: imagination and narration of cities by artists, architects, writers
findings.quote: The Situationist International (SI) was a group of artists,filmmakers, writers and others active mostly in Paris from 195x-197x. They have influenced the way artists, architects, writers and othersimagine and narrate their cities.

findings.antecedent: unitary urbanism (combined use of arts and techniques)
findings.consequent: construction of a unified milieu in dynamic relation with experiments in behaviour
findings.quote: The approach called unitary urbanism proposed a “combined use of arts and techniques as means contributing to the construction of a unified milieu in dynamic relation with experiments in behaviour.”

findings.consequent: people blind to a living critique of cities
findings.quote: They held the position that contemporary city-planning has made people blind to “a living critique of this manipulation of cities and their inhabitants, a critique fuelled by all the tensions of everyday life.

findings.consequent: people drawn by attractions of terrain and encounters
findings.quote: “In a derive one or more persons during a certain period drop their relations, their work and leisure activities, and all their other usual motives for movement and action, and let themselves be drawn by the attractions of the terrain and the encounters they find there.”

findings.source: Section 5.2 Anonymity and Public Spaces, p. 13
findings.quote: “Public space protects us from an excess of intimacy. [it] is a space of great anonymity.”

findings.antecedent: surveillance by video cameras and I-card (in Indian cities)
findings.source: Section 5.2 Anonymity and Public Spaces, p. 13
findings.quote: But with surveillance by video cameras and I-card now being very common even in Indian cities,that anonymity is being lost and is being replaced by a perpetual self-consciousness which is not very helpful for free self-expression or intermingling with other people.

findings.consequent: seeking 'cracks and vacancies' in State control and surveillance
findings.source: Section 5.1 Participation in the Urban Dialogue and the Autonomy of PublicAction, p. 12
findings.quote: The tactic of the TAZ is a process of seeking “cracks and vacancies” in the supposedly omnipresent, omnipotent State with its many mechanisms for surveillance and control of experience.

findings.source: Section 5.1 Participation in the Urban Dialogue and the Autonomy of PublicAction, p. 11
findings.quote: The Internet and the software world saw a partial opening-up between the relationships between these two players, due to the failure of existing relationships to come up with successful products.

findings.consequent: development teams continually open to user demands, requests, preferences
findings.source: Section 5.1 Participation in the Urban Dialogue and the Autonomy of PublicAction, p. 12
findings.quote: The “permanent beta” allows development teams to be continually open to user demands and requests and preferences by changing their development paradigm.

findings.consequent: social knowledge and opportunities for active participation
findings.source: Section 5.1 Participation in the Urban Dialogue and the Autonomy of PublicAction, p. 12
findings.quote: The imagined temporary spaces create social knowledge and offer opportunities for active participation, rather than temporary spaces for an event-based leisure society.

findings.antecedent: people carrying more of their lives into the outdoors
findings.consequent: desire to configure outdoors to their taste and preference
findings.quote: When people start carrying more of their lives into the outdoors, they will definitely want to configure outdoors to their taste and preference.
Creating engaging situations which are simple, fun and socially productive for them and at the same time get them involved in a mesh of wide-ranging concerns is a worthwhile pursuit.

findings.antecedent: city-dwellers feeling responsible, empowered, playful and concerned toward their city
findings.consequent: relief from disenfranchised, passive observer status
findings.quote: As city-dwellers. being in a situations where we feel responsible,empowered, playful and concerned toward our city would be welcome and quite a relief from the current status of the individual as a disenfranchised, passive observer of the spectacle which the state chooses to churn out.

limitations: The projects described are 'ongoing' and not fully realized or evaluated yet (p. 14).
The paper's scope limits detailed discussion of the proposed technology for each component (p. 90).
Alternative ways of doing this (implementing the framework) need to be explored further (p. 90).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper introduces CitySpinning, a conceptual framework for public art interventions that re-interprets unused urban spaces in Bangalore. It proposes making these spaces more configurable by individuals, drawing inspiration from free software and creative commons movements. Key findings suggest that collective control over sensory ambiance through multiple sensors can create more engaging experiences, and ongoing dialogue between citizens and planners can prevent urban planning 'glitches'. The framework aims to foster social knowledge and active participation in shaping the city, offering a relief from the passive observer status. Limitations include the ongoing nature of the described projects and the paper's scope, which restricts detailed discussion of the underlying technology.

paper_metadata.title: Museums and the Embodied Mind: Sensory Engagement with Artworks and Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Museums and the Embodied Mind: Sensory Engagement with Artworks and Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractA museum or gallery is usually thought of as a space containing objects arranged in a chosen way. Understanding the multisensory factors that modulate an audience's experiences of artworks in their settings offers museum curators and architects opportunities to enhance visitors’ sensory engagement with their collections. Barry C Smith, Director of the Institute of Philosophy, Centre for the Study of the Senses, School of Advanced Study, University of London, considers a number of ways this can happen.
